newsitem.title: UK: Russia's eye on French franc Eurobond raises brows.
newsitem.headline: Russia's eye on French franc Eurobond raises brows.

text.p: Russia's plans to tap the French franc Eurobond sector surprised bankers on Tuesday who said the French investor base could be once-bitten- twice-shy following the Tsarist debt dispute.
"As long as the Tsarist debt issue hangs over us, we cannot do anything for Russia in French francs," a syndicate manager at a French bank in Paris said.
"But the French government is probably having talks with the Russian finance officials to clear it up... until they are authorised by the French Treasury, they will not be able to do it."
First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said in a magazine interview published on Tuesday Russia would enter the French franc market after resolving the issue of debt to France.
Key investment banks familiar with Russian debt were surprised at the announcement as they had not been informed of a possible mandate and details were vague.
Last year Russia signed an agreement with France to repay around $400 million to some 400,000 holders of Tsarist bonds, which were issued before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.
But some bankers said there were still barriers to overcome such as negative sentiment among the French investor base and their lack of emerging market appetite.
"I am amazed, I don't think French francs is the obvious choice for Russia," a dealer said.
Russia launched its debut Eurobond last November -- a $1.0 billion offering. It was priced to yield 345 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes.
The second issue, a 2.0 billion mark seven-year bond, was priced at 370 b.p. over Bunds.
But a dealer said a French franc bond would be "a tough sell".
"I can buy more liquid dollar issues and swap them into French francs, and dollars have a much bigger retail pick-up then French francs," he added.
Another dealer said Russia would "get away with anything if they paid the right rate".
Russia has said it would launch another two bonds this year raising at least $2.0 billion, Finance Minister Alexander Livshits has said.
Livshits said at least one of the issues would be denominated in dollars.
